video_title: Philip & Allan Maymin – Compounding Through Risk, Not Return (S7E35)
transcript: Well, gentlemen, are you ready? Ready. Yes. OK. 3, 2, 1, let's go. Greetings to everyone. I'm Corey Hofstein, and this is the Flirting with Models podcast, which lifts the curtain to see the human factor behind quantitative strategies. Corey Hofstein is co-founder and chief investment officer of Newfound Research. Due to industry norms, he will not discuss any of Newfound Research's funds on this podcast. All opinions expressed by podcast participants are solely their own and do not reflect the position of Newfound Research. This podcast is for informational purposes only and should not be relied upon as the basis for investment decisions . Newfound Research clients may hold positions in the securities discussed in this podcast. For more information, visit thinknewfound.com. In this episode, I speak with Philip and Allan Maiman, co-heads of global asset allocation at Janus Henderson. Philip and Allan lead the asset allocation group, founded at Janus Henderson over a decade ago by Nobel laureate Myron Scholes, and they came to this by surprisingly different paths. Philip—through LTCM, academia, and behavioral analytics. Allan— through high-frequency trading, derivatives, and proprietary trading operations. At the heart of their approach is a simple but unconventional idea. As Philip said during our previous conversation: "People live in a middle- income world, and they shouldn't ." For investors, compound growth is important, and the brothers believe that the most reliable way to improve it is not by chasing higher returns, but by managing risk. Setbacks destroy aggregate growth, and avoiding them is a more effective lever. They connect theory with practice through the options market. Call and put options contain the market's collective forward-looking views on risk, making them one of the richest sources of information for an asset manager. We discuss how to extract these signals and extend them across over 4,000 assets to build portfolios aligned with client goals, not benchmarks. Enjoy my conversation with Philip and Allan Maiman. Phil and Allan, welcome to the show. This is the first time. This is the first time I have brothers together on a show. I hope we see brotherly love. We won't see any sibling rivalry like we would if I invited my brother, and we'll have a great episode. So thank you very much for joining me. Very excited about this release. Mutually. Thank you for inviting us. Since there are two of you, we will have to make a somewhat abbreviated introduction. I'll quickly try to go through your biographies. This may be a bit like a sprint, but Phil, I want to start with you. You both have taken very interesting paths to get to where you are today. Phil, you start a little earlier than your brother , but your journey, which began with LTCM in the 90s, eventually led to a PhD. For a while, you ran your own hedge fund. You've worked a little in academia. You worked in behavioral analytics at Essentia, and then joined Janus Henderson 4 years ago. It's a pretty winding path. Maybe you can see some logic in it for me. Allan and I were just talking about it. This is like the main event of the day. We communicate almost every day, and it's always nice. He is wonderful. This was my journey. So, I started with LTCM, worked at several other hedge funds, including my own. At some point I got my PhD, and when you get your degree, you have to go straight to academia. Well, because I was working, and all of this is classified information. They don't understand this. So you need to go right away, while you have that one piece of work, your dissertation—something that the system is ready to evaluate. They say, "Okay, now you can be a professor." "And then do whatever you want." My first job in academia was at NYU, financial engineering. Then financial engineering turned into something like finance and analytics. A line of research emerged at the MIT Sloan conference on sports analytics . Allan and I and our friend started writing articles for him. That's how I grew from finance to sports analytics. So 4 years ago I joined Alan, Myron and the rest of our team. It was just incredible. This is the best possible place. But my very specific question to you is: LTCM is known as the great collapse. I'm curious about your perception of risk before working at LTCM and how LTCM shaped your view of what risk is and portfolio risk after that crash. I traded derivatives on stocks. Equity derivatives were different from most fixed income instruments and other asset classes that LTCM traded. The world was different at that time. It's hard to remember. You know , there was no margin at all. Unsecured financing was used . So you were literally trying to find alpha and scale it up as much as possible, hoping it was uncorrelated. The one thing that everyone has learned, of course, is that in the "tails" the correlations tend to unity. Perfectly. This is a very important lesson. But, to be fair, on the equity derivatives desk, we worked with convertible bonds, warrants, and things like that, so there was always risk. Even without margin, you still have to think about efficiency relative to the risk you are taking. The biggest takeaway for me was the correlations in the “tails, ” and that the “tails” can be—and this later became the focus of my dissertation— self-limitations for arbitrage. Even if you can do more, sometimes it's better not to . Okay, Alan, now it's your turn to answer the uncomfortable questions. Like your brother, you had quite a few career changes before you happily ended up where you are. So let's go through them. You started with quantitative execution algorithms at the very dawn of the high-frequency trading era. Then you moved on to Platinum Grove. You were doing derivatives on the sell side at SocGen. And then—an internal hedge fund at Alliance Bernstein. Finally, worked at a prop trading firm before joining Janus Henderson. In our previous conversation, you noted that most statistical arbitrage and HFT strategies, and I quote , “worked better when everything was falling apart .” I find this an interesting observation, and I was hoping you could expand on this thought, building on your brother's words and reflections on the risks. So a significant part of our conversation today will be devoted to risks. Given your experience, how did you come to this conclusion and what do you think it means for the behavior of markets in stressful situations? I would approach it this way: my experience is more related to development. So early in my career in finance, to be useful, I did quantitative execution, HFT, and writing pricing tools at an investment bank —these were ways to get a foothold in the industry and create value through writing code. Interestingly, I was lucky enough to survive part of the events of 2008 , but the moment that I remember most is the " flash crash" of 2010. When I say things worked better during the crash, I mean that many statistical arbitrage and HFT strategies on short timeframes benefit by taking advantage of an uninformed order flow where people are forced to trade mechanically. I know that after the 2010 collapse, there was a lot of mutual accusations. I remember some retail investor taking the brunt of the blow, but what was most interesting to me was that when the sales started to skyrocket, people were forced to keep trading. Whether it was through delta hedging and their gamma positions requiring selling, or through day trading ETFs, what struck me was that it had become a kind of self-reinforcing loop. I find it extremely interesting that many of these short-term trading styles are related to liquidity, whether you are creating it or consuming it. When you are the sole liquidity provider, you can set any price. So if we trace your career, Alan, you started in HFT and now you've come to asset allocation. I'm sure some of my previous guests from the HFT space might take offense to this , but I was hoping you could flesh out this idea, as I find it controversial but insightful. And again , I think this will help set the stage for the rest of our conversation. I think this statement is common quantum wisdom. Of course, I agree that there are many smart people working in short time slots , and, in fact, that's where many of the technologies we use now originated. For example, Solar Flare and similar things in the AI ​​world. I think a better distinction would be "explained" versus " unexplained." I'm not necessarily saying " linear" versus " nonlinear" or anything like that. You can certainly use very fast nonlinear models on very short timescales. But perhaps you are less interested in the explainability of short-term trading, while on longer horizons this explainability is necessary. Your Sharpe ratios naturally return to reality, and you need some anchor to understand why you stay within a certain strategy. So , if you have explainability, economic justification, and something to rely on , you can hold onto a trading strategy that is temporarily underperforming due to market noise. So, let's talk a little about Janus Henderson. Phil, Myron Scholes founded the asset allocation group over a decade ago. You mentioned that you talk to him every day. Now the two of you lead the asset allocation team. Can you tell us a little about who your clients are and what services you provide them? Yes, we have a mixed client base: both institutional and retail investors, as we have a mutual fund available to retail clients. Our shared philosophy is to improve compounded earnings, which I'm sure we'll talk about in more detail later. In particular, we care about providing you with a solution. We don't just say, "This is the only thing we can trade or offer you." What is your problem? What are your goals? What are your limitations? Let's create something with dynamic risk management, our tools, signals and philosophy that will help you achieve what you want. There is a difference between goals and results. They sound like synonyms, but they are different things. Goals are what you strive for and what you need, and then you check the results: are we delivering on that promise? Are you getting the expected excess income for the reasons you expected, not just because of luck? So that's exactly what we're trying to do. We start by asking each client what they are trying to achieve and why. If you just ask anyone, "Hey, I want more money and no risk," well, that's obvious. But what's the money for? When will you need it? What will you do if you lose money? How much can you afford? And then we adapt the risk and the portfolio structure to try to meet the client's goal within their constraints. I know that the idea of compound interest is extremely important to the way you all think about portfolio construction. In our previous conversation, you laid out a logical chain of reasoning: Everyone wants more money. More money comes from better compound interest, and while you can try to improve your expected return, your quote was, "Risk is easier to manage." Can you talk a little bit about why risk is a more manageable lever for improving your compound interest compared to your expected return? That's a great question, because there are a lot of reasons. First, there's a certain anomaly or conundrum. If you have a scenario with a positive average return, right? You have a certain alpha. That's your average return. You actually want to make more money in the future. So you want your compound interest rate to be higher. And the compound interest rate is different from the average by the amount of the risk premium. That's right. That means that for any average return, no matter how good your average alpha is, if I add enough noise to it, you're going to start losing money. No matter how much alpha you have, there's a level of risk that suddenly you're in a "good news and bad news" situation. The good news: our alpha is stable, we're still delivering 5% average return . The bad news: you're bankrupt because of the risk. It's harder to make up for your losses after you've lost money. That's right. If you think about it , compound interest rate is average return minus risk. Average interest rate -- I don't use that word often , and I've never heard it used very often. When I do, it's always related to alpha. Alpha is variable . You never hear about variability, right? It's not a very common word, but it describes the essence of alpha perfectly. You can spend your entire career —short or long—and suddenly wake up one day and realize that what you thought was the source of alpha has disappeared. The world has changed, moved on, your contacts have disappeared, and the knowledge you thought you were gaining has suddenly evaporated. With risk management, it's different. If you manage risk, you expect change and you can build not a changing source of knowledge, but a constantly growing base. You know how to operate in different conditions. That's not going to go away. We're not suddenly in a world where there's only one environment. No, conditions are always changing. Another reason—Bob Merton. In 1980, he wrote an article. One of the most memorable things was a great article, but even in the appendix he gave a very important observation. The observation was this: in a purely statistical sense, how confident do you have to be and how far back do you have to go to distinguish alpha, the average return, from zero. And you have to look quite far back. It all depends on the length of time. It doesn't matter whether you break down the data into weekly or daily returns . That doesn't matter. All that matters is the beginning, the end, and the total length of the period. So you have to look far enough back, sometimes decades, to be confident that what you're measuring is statistically different from zero. So at some point you analyze whether IBM has a positive alpha, comparing the returns of the 1970s . But that's not the IBM that's today. What's the point? So alpha is variable. It's hard to measure. Okay, what about risk? Risk, as he shows in that appendix, and as you well know, the finer you slice the returns, the better you measure risk. That's more reliable and more confident. You don't have to look far back. You just go from monthly data to weekly, daily, hourly data, and you get increasingly accurate risk estimates. So, when combined, these things make it easier to measure risk, reflect the variability of the environment, allow you to accumulate knowledge and plan for the long term. That's why it's a more manageable, simpler, and more important lever for generating aggregate returns. Allen, the process that you and your team have created is based on what you call a dynamic risk management process. When most people in the industry hear about risk, when we talk about published risk papers, traditionally we talk about volatility. What does risk mean to you, both conceptually and in terms of actual measurement? We think of risk as the probability of not achieving a client's objectives, not just the degree of portfolio volatility. If we take a goal-oriented approach and can identify different scenarios for a particular client or mandate, we We view risk as the probability that a client's expectations will not be met. When people think about risk through the lens of volatility, they run into another problem: volatility weighs both gains and losses equally. We try to separate out the upside risk, which may actually be desirable. The downside risk is what we want to avoid. From our perspective, we view risk not necessarily as a measure of volatility, but rather as a measure of probability: what are the possible outcomes and how can we steer them toward what the client wants and away from what they want to avoid? I know that one of the key elements of your process is analyzing the options market information embedded in puts and calls to assess risk, and that applies not just to the major asset classes but, if I'm not mistaken, to the thousands of assets and securities that you use to build your portfolio. Can you talk a little bit about how you use options chains and the information embedded in them to measure upside and downside risks and how does that affect your process? The best thing about the options market is that it provides a forward-looking assessment of the upside and downside potential of a particular asset. In addition, a premium must be exchanged to execute a trade . So for the options market to work, participants really need to back up their words with real money. As a result , by analyzing information, trades, and prices, we can see where market participants think an asset will go over a period of time. This information is incredibly rich . It spans many different time horizons and many different strike prices. In other words, you can see across the entire distribution of possible outcomes over different time periods how likely the market is that an asset will achieve a particular outcome. We can take this information and convert it into the probability of that asset moving up or determining the upside risk. Similarly, what is the downside risk or “left tail” risk for a particular asset? By tracking this information over time and, importantly, its correlation, we can see how the potential the rise of an asset relative to its decline. This information is very valuable because it is the market distribution of returns for a particular asset, as implied by the price. This helps us to build a portfolio for a client, shifting it towards assets with greater potential for growth and avoiding assets with a high risk of decline. Anyone who has had classical training as a quantitative analyst or has worked with derivatives will immediately notice that options are priced on what is called a risk- neutral measure, and you are trying to use it to assess real risks. The P-measure. These are different measures, and they do not necessarily always agree with each other. So I am wondering what you think about this "P versus Q" issue when using signals derived from options. What is the biggest difference between these two measures? Of course, it is drift, right? And that is what Fisher and Myron showed in 1973. Drift is quite different. It is risk- neutral in one case and has an arbitrary The rest of the distribution may be different. However, you can try to simulate the situation , assuming what the real indicator is, and then determine the risk-neutral one. Almost all of this difference is due to the change in drift. The shape of the distribution is quite resistant to changes in the measure. As Alan said, we have an upside risk and a downside risk. It is not by chance that we ignore the middle. The whole philosophy is built on the idea that the middle does not matter. It is the "tails" that matter. You can discard... We have an article that proves this. You can discard the middle 80% of the distribution, and your risk will remain essentially the same. You can have a correlation of 80 to 90%. 80-90% of the risk still remains. The " tails" are important, and options value these "tails" very, very well. And it is these shapes that we use as signals. And remember, as Alan said, we do not take one number in one day as some ultimate truth. We look at changes in that signal relative to itself and to others. Things don't always work 100%, but the risk we don't really worry about is P versus Q, the risk-neutral world versus the real world, because it would have to be different enough to contradict all the parts of our process that translate into a smart signal. And that's totally fine. See what Alan says we're doing? To summarize, if suddenly and over a long period of time people are buying a lot more calls and a lot less puts, that's interesting information. Despite P versus Q, there's something to that . When more people are buying options for up, backing it with their own money, than for down, that's a signal . If no other asset is doing that , then that asset is special. Your actual pick is the 90th percentile of the notional value at risk along with its counterpart for up. Why the 90th percentile, and not, say, The 95th or the 99th? Probably the best and most straightforward way to answer that is to say that for any parameter in any quantum system, you have to choose something. And for us, the 90th percentile, or the 10th delta, is that " extreme" option that makes some sense. There's usually volume there, there's prices there, and the spreads aren't crazy. It's extreme, but it's not too niche. It's not something that's extremely disconnected from the market. It provides a yardstick by which we can draw a line. Anything after that is either bullish or bearish to us. Once you cross that point , you're in the tail scenario. And understanding what the expected, average, or typical experience is in that scenario is the value that we're trying to extract from the options market. What does the "tail" look like, whether it's bullish or bearish? We know for sure: once you cross that barrier and If you're going through the 90th percentile, you're definitely in the tail . So for us, highlighting what that experience looks like is a signal that we're trying to get from the options market. Let's talk a little bit about how you actually use these metrics to build portfolios . I want to start by going back to your discussion about providing solutions for clients. You're actually taking an approach that's more objective or outcome-oriented for your clients. What does that actually mean in practice? When you sit down with a new client, what do you actually ask them at the very beginning, and how do their answers shape the rest of the portfolio building process? One of the perspectives that we encourage them to come to in their answers -- and it's sometimes very natural for people, and sometimes it can be a little new -- is drawdown. What's the maximum drawdown that you could take and still recover? And it's different for each person, depending on what they're willing to accept. Sometimes it's a new question for them because they might just We lived in a world where we always had a benchmark portfolio of 60/40, and we just wanted to beat it, and that was it. But when you start asking that question, you start to realize: Where did 60/40 come from? Why is this some God-given standard? And it's based on a very smart thing: Look at stocks in times of turmoil. Historically, they've fallen 50%. But we can't afford a 50% drawdown because that would mean we have to double our capital next year, and that's too much risk, and we have investors and clients, and that's just not going to happen. But we could afford a 30% drawdown. We can recover from that. We have a long enough planning horizon, we can do it. So how do you get to a 30% drawdown? Well, if you're only 60% in stocks and you assume that fixed income is fairly uncorrelated in these turbulent times, then you get 30% drawdown. That's what the 60/40 portfolio is supposed to convey , and it's kind of a proxy that people have come to because they're really looking for something like 30% drawdown. Once you start to pull that mindset out, they can be more specific. Well, okay, maybe it's 30%. Maybe it's time to increase or decrease that a little bit . Maybe we'll want to change it over time. But if drawdown is what matters, then we can start to move away from the solution that looks at the correlation of fixed income with stocks as a hedge. The three of us, and I'm sure many of your listeners, grew up in a world for the last few decades, up until a few years ago, where the law of nature was that stocks and bonds were negatively correlated. Bonds go up, stocks go down, and vice versa. Which is the reality. It's a new law of physics. And then 2022 came along. year, and of course it turns out not to be. In fact, if you look at the last 100 to 150 years, most of the time they're positively correlated. Which makes perfect sense. How can two asset classes with the largest expected positive returns in the world be negatively correlated? You've got some arbitrage going on here. That can't be the case in the future. So instead of statically solving the problem of drawdown, which is the real problem , if you accept that drawdown is the main question: "This is our maximum drawdown budget," and of course we want to make as much profit as possible, but this is our budget, then you can start thinking dynamically. How can we dynamically manage our exposures to achieve our goal of making as much profit as possible within this particular drawdown limit? Does the risk seem worth it or not? the most obvious goal , besides the fact that people may have a return goal that is perhaps a little more difficult to achieve directly. All else being equal, when you have a large universe or menu of options for names that you want to shift your portfolio in or out of, it seems extremely sensible to consider the tax impact of a particular name. So, all else being equal , if you are going to sell an asset to get cash to buy another, it is likely to be more profitable to sell the one that has a tax loss compared to the others. Ultimately, tax- efficient investing is simply an optimization function that is about some tax deferral. This is for the client who wants to maintain control and certainty about tax time. We're not taking taxes out of the equation by any means, but it helps smooth out the timing component. So if there's a big windfall or something like that, it can help to defer short-term income into long-term income. This " locked in" portfolio problem is becoming more and more common today, with the market constantly rising, especially given the skew toward certain names. There's almost never an opportunity to lock in a profit , because prices have gone up so much. Some of the tools that are available to you are, as you said, taking both " long" and " short" positions, which allows you to find opportunities throughout most of the market cycle for these types of trades. And finally, I would add that ultimately it all comes down to a trade-off. As Phil mentioned, it all starts with the client's objectives first and foremost . And what exactly does the client want to achieve with a particular mandate? Can we create a generalized version of what the opportunity set is in terms of prospective risk? And this is the ratio, the expected return in the "tail" divided by the expected loss in the "tail" for the portfolio. This is the bulge you want to create. When you have a convexity, or a skewness, because these predictions of future performance that come out of the options markets are actually very good predictors of what's going to happen in the future, studies support that, and we've done some of them, so we know that the implied risk measures, of course, the implied volatility absorbs all the other risk predictors. Why? Because if there was additional information that could be useful, option prices would be adjusted, otherwise arbitrage would arise. So, we know that implicit predictions are better. This is also true for gains and losses in terms of expected gains in the tails and expected losses in the tails. So we have this research, this belief, and this understanding that the options markets are roughly telling you the answer to your original question about the risk- neutral world versus the real world. We know that they do predict what usually happens with changes in upside and downside risks. Perfectly. You get more participation in the rise and less in the fall. This is the Holy Grail. Not alpha, as we discussed, alpha is variable, but it is this kind of convexity—that is the goal. If you can have it, it's sustainable, long-lasting, and transferable. This is the goal.
